chapter: Club culture, radio and the rise of R&B
title: Club Desire's decline, gambling, fashion, bop and black radio
summary: Stephens explains why Club Desire faded, then ranges over Prohibition-era bars, gambling and pawn shops, zoot-style clothes, hip slang, bop, Elvis and the Beatles, black radio, second lines and benevolent clubs, and New Orleans R&B artists and his own start as a disc jockey.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Did that cause the demise of that club? Because I don't think it...

I don't think so. No. No. I don't think it caused the demise of the club. I think things started changing with... You see, Club Desire was down in the Ninth Ward. But you had the Dewdrop, the Robin Hood, and all of these Johnny-come-lately clubs, which were just beginning to hit their stride to develop new entertainment. Then, like I said, you had the Coliseum Arena, which was in the central part of the city. You had the ILA Club, which was in the French Quarter. You had all of these things jumping against Charlie Armstead's Club Desire. But the Desire was mostly like a neighborhood club, in a sense. It never reached the peak of sensationalism like the Dewdrop and the Robin Hood in its state. But it still was a mainstay down in the Ninth Ward. Because many of the shows, when the entertainers got tired of hanging around the Hurricane, the Dewdrop, the Robin Hood, and the other clubs, they would finally wind their way down to Club Desire. But I think somewhere in time things started changing. They started building new areas all across the city of New Orleans. You had slowly the coming of integration. The war was beginning to end. And people was going off, was moving. They were moving all over the city of New Orleans. But I can't say any one particular thing other than what I stated just a few minutes ago as to what caused Club Desire to fade away. But Charlie Armstead took ill some time back. I think that had a lot to do with it because he never could get anybody in his family or to hire any professional people to run the club to make it the sensation that it was. When Dave Bartholomew opened, then came Billy Eckstein, one of the shows. When Billy Eckstein came twice, but I am seeded, I think the first time that Billy Eckstein came, he am seeded that show. And then a lot of other things started happening. But like I said earlier, I was getting ready to tell you about Buddy Johnson and Arthur Priceock. And then Louis Jordan. Of course, we can never forget, say too much about the Godfather of all the music. The world's greatest ambassador, Louis Armstrong, who came to New Orleans many a time in the 1930s. He played that concert. I think I showed you a program down at the, not the hall, but that naval facility down in the Ninth Ward. And then, of course, here we had coming, getting ready to move 40s into the 50s. Things were wide open. The throttle was wide open. More and more clubs were beginning to open up. See, when we go back to 1933, that's when Prohibition came. What's that? Right. The Volstead Act was beginning to die. And then a lot of clubs opened. They started calling themselves Beer Paulus. Then eventually in the black neighborhoods, they started calling them Beer Gardens and different things like that. The names began to change. And Beer Emporiums, different names were, it was really, really fun. And then, well, Rampart Street was in its glory because, you see, you could walk up and down. Then Gambling was in Vogue. Gambling was down at the Club Pelican. Then you had Gambling at many other facilities in and around the city of New Orleans. And then you had the lottery, the long list ticket with about the 10 to 12 numbers on it. Just so many things were happening. And then you had down on Rampart Street, you had more pawn shops on Connell Street than any other place at any other time in history. Because musicians sometimes would get into the gambling thing from the house of Uncle Al over to the Pelican down to many other clubs all over the city. Uptown, they had clubs like the Brown Derby. They used to gamble in the back. And then Coon Kent Joan up on the South Street in the back of his club. He and Fast Life Eddie, Treacherous Slim, Big Dipper. I'm trying to think of some of the guys, the Whispering Boots. All those guys were big-time gamblers. And some of them were pimps. They had women on the streets. New Orleans was in its glory days when you go back to the 30s and to the 40s. And an intermixture of the music, the jazz perpetuated a lot of the things. Because blacks were beginning to wear big diamonds. And they were beginning to wear beautiful clothes and so forth and so on. And then when we go back to the 40s, I'm thinking about when Gone with the Wind came out. And then stormy weather hit the screen with Cab Calloway. Then the long coat with the chain with the 27-inch knee and the 12-inch bottom. And the long coats and the big white hats. Boy, those were the days of good time. And I guess I was one of them also. Lewis Johnson, myself, Charles Dimes. We were the pinwheels of the guys who loved to wear the Gone with the Wind outfit and the big hats. Now, the big hats wasn't sold in New Orleans right away. I had to send off to Chicago to get my big hat. Because I can remember in 1940, 42, 43, when I first heard Count Basie's band singing Going to Chicago with, I tried to think of a gentleman who sang Mr. Five by Five. Look, I had a lot of fun growing up listening to jazz music and blues and so forth and so on. And I think it gave me the will to live, to want to do somebody, to be somebody, rather. Because I tell you, Tad, we didn't have a lot of money then. Things were cheap, like you could buy eggs with a nickel a dozen. Some stores would sell them two dozen for a nickel when they would stay in the store for maybe an extra week or so. Bacon was a nickel a pound. You could get five pounds of potatoes for six cents and things like that. Then we had the token that came in somewhere back in the 1930s and 40s. Well, so many things were beginning to happen, but I'm trying to get the interrelationship between music, the style of the clothing, the social methodology that was prevalent at that time, how people would, and then new languages were falling into focus. Where you at? What's happening? Hey, baby, let's get it together. Beat you down to a low deuce of blunders on a mellow QT. What's the drift, baby? Yeah, everything is cool. Then the verbiage started finding its way into music. He's got it together. Yeah, he's a cool dude. Then here comes Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Park, and these guys, and here comes Bop in the 40s. And people say, what is Bop? This is a fast overdrive beat that had jazz and blues overtones, but most people couldn't dance to it because this was the time when a guy with a saxophone or a trumpet or a guitar could pick up the pace, but your feet could not emancipate the structure of what the music was all about. And then Bop music didn't take off right away with the majority of the people. It was more, shall we say, a character reference of a musician who expedited his skill or craftsmanship as an individual in front of a group or in front of his band to say, well, here, I'm the headliner, and I'm going to showcase my talent with all of these various riffs. Sometimes the pianists did it. Sometimes the saxophones did it. Well, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, these guys, they highlighted this thing. Of course, there were many other musicians who got involved into the Bop kind of thing, but Bop didn't, shall we say, go over like ordinary jazz or blues. But here we come as we get into the 80s, 70s, and things started changing again. You had a revolutionary structure with a slowly drift of integration slowly coming. And you have guys like Elvis Presley. Many blacks didn't pick up on Elvis Presley right away. But Elvis Presley was a lover of black people, and he emulated a lot of blacks. And he will tell anybody, if he was living today, that many a time he had many black friends that he got involved with and played music with. And some people have records of it. I don't have any recollection of it, but I read about it in certain professional publications and newspapers, where Elvis Presley got into a jam session with him and a few other musicians. But all in all, then along come the Beatles from Europe. Then you had another thing beginning to happen, whether we covered this or not, Ted, I don't know. But music that was played on the radio in the 40s from the black side was called race music. And somewhere in time, as we started slowly moving into the 50s, black radio stations started developing all across the country, from WDIA in Memphis, Tennessee, and then you had other stations, and then eventually WMROY in New Orleans, and then WBOK. And then black talent was beginning to explode across the horizons. And then like station WLAC out of Nashville, a 50,000-watt station started playing the black talent, and many of the black artists of its day got its popularity from WLAC, which was a 50,000-watt station like WWL here in New Orleans. And WWL was not playing the music like WLAC. But however, WWL did highlight good jazz music, Moonglow with Martin that night. Dick Martin would come on at midnight, and from 12 until about 3 in the morning, Dick Martin would let it all hang out. And I'm sure with the 50,000-watt station, that helped to perpetuate the structure of jazz and many given geographical areas at that time. And let's see what else happened. Then we would reflect back. We didn't get too much into that, Ted. Now, here's what happened with jazz in the city of New Orleans. We had a lot of musicians who didn't read music as such, but they were gifted with something called the ear for music. Sometimes musicians would pick up a horn and start blowing, pick up a guitar or a banjo mostly at that particular time. Then the drums, and we had what was known as the street parades. And then we had what was known as the second line venture. Now, a lot of people may not live by this, but as I read and look back, all of this, well, some did come from Africa. Years ago, when they buried a black in Africa, they would march behind without any music as such, but just a skin or piece of hide over an empty piece of bulk, and it would make a noise like it was really a drum as the way they saw it. And then they would march back and go on back home. But somewhere in time, with the development of education and new instruments and people beginning to learn how to play music, some did, some would read, some could not. But there was an amalgamation of people in New Orleans for some strange reason. By accident, the second line was born because New Orleans was small at one time, and you could walk to the graveyards before the graveyards were on the outskirts of the city. And people would just follow behind and walk. Then you had the birth of what is known as the benevolent associations, where you would spend maybe five cents a week or 25 cents a month, and you could be buried. And your family would get like maybe $5 or $10 by that time period, some $25. One thing I never discussed yet was on the West Bank of the River, one of the largest organizations of a marching club was the Wolves Club, which was over on the West Bank of the River. This was the first organization that was the owner of its own facility. They had their own club that they paid for. The New Orleans people didn't own their own club. They would just fall in and form an organization and say, here we are, and they would have a meeting at some bar or some lounge or some private home. But the Wolves Club on the West Bank of the River, they had their first organization, the building that they owned. Then in McDonoughville, which was a part of Gretna at that time, they also had a benevolent association. I can't think of the name of it. It was in Gretna, but it was in the McDonoughville section area, which was founded by John McDonough years ago. So many things were happening. So many changes were beginning to take place. And then all of a sudden we had what was known as an explosion of talent with the coming of black radio. You had people like Edgar Blanchard and the Gondoliers. Then Larry Darnell came to town. I don't know exactly where Larry Darnell came from. But then you had the Lincoln Theater. You had the Palace Theater. They all were going strong. You had people like Chevy Newsom who came to town. Then Ethel Morris, she was already here. B. Booker, she was already here. Then you had jazz blues giants like Smiler Lewis, who was beginning to make recordings. Joe, Mr. Google Eye August. He recorded for Columbia. I can remember playing some of his records because I'm the first disc jockey he brought them to because I started in 1948, 49, playing jazz music. I'm the first black jazz disc jockey in the city of New Orleans. And then from then on, then you had the Johnson Brothers. Then there was a fellow by the name of Theodore Johnson who was a balladeer. He was singing with Dave Bartholomew and his band. That's when I first met them on Ramport Street in the old studio where Casa Mombatassa made all the recordings years ago. Then there was Dave Bartholomew's big band, the Johnson Brothers. See, these people came behind Sidney Desveen and Jim Walters and all the other bands before them. Then Kid Ori. All of these people, they handed things down to the young set was beginning to come into focus. Singers like Tammy Lynn, Jewel King, then Tommy Ridgely, then Fats Domino, who probably made more recordings than any one talent out of the city of New Orleans that I could think of. And when he and Dave Bartholomew got together, there was another explosion and there was an amalgamation of very beautiful talent. And both are alive today and today, well, both of them have traveled all over the world. And they have been tremendous ambassadors for the city of New Orleans, just like Louis Armstrong was in his day when he was alive. And then you had the development of what is known as gospel music, the Zion harmonizers. When they first walk into the old WMLY studio, I can never forget I was the announcer and I helped to put them on the air. And today we are the very best of friends. And then you had WBOK radio station, which was beginning to expose a lot of talent. And then you had the stations, both were beginning to play popular music. Jazz was taking a back seat, but popular music and gospel music was beginning to highlight more and to focus much more so than jazz. Now jazz music was beginning to play, or be played maybe twice a week, sometimes on the weekend. But every day they had the music that was beginning to play. This was the birth of what we would call rock and roll was beginning to come into focus. This was before rap now. We're talking into the 60s, 70s, 80s, and 90s. All right, then you had, well.
